summary: Area is the amount of two-dimensional surface inside a bounded region, measured by counting how many unit squares (the usual chosen unit of area) cover the figure with no gaps or overlaps. A unit square has area 1 square unit; a figure covered by 12 unit squares has area 12 square units. The concept must be held distinct from perimeter (the distance around) and understood as unchanged when the same squares are rearranged (area is additive and conserved under recomposition). Answers should always carry square-unit language.
misconceptions: Confuses area with perimeter / length — judges the 'bigger' shape by how far it stretches or the distance around, not the surface covered.
Undifferentiated 'bigger' — calls a longer or taller shape bigger by one dimension without coordinating the 2D covering.
Thinks rearranging the same squares into a new shape changes the amount of area.
Gives area as a bare number without square units, or counts squares with gaps/overlaps.

activities.title: Cover, count, and separate area from perimeter
steps: Fill a figure drawn on squared paper with unit squares, snapping them edge-to-edge with no gaps or overlaps, and count them to state the area, e.g. 'area = 12 square units'.

Trace the boundary of the SAME shape separately, stepping round the edge and counting the unit lengths, and record the perimeter in unit lengths. This is a different kind of measure from the area. For a 12-square figure the perimeter number is also different (at least 14), but for some shapes the two numbers can match: a 4-by-4 square has area 16 square units and perimeter 16 units. Even then they measure different things.
Say aloud that the squares INSIDE measure area while the steps AROUND measure perimeter — two different measures of the same shape.

Rearrange the same set of (e.g. 12) tiles, joined edge-to-edge, into a long strip. Re-count the covering squares (still 12), then re-count the perimeter and compare. For example, a 3-by-4 rectangle has perimeter 14 units, but a 1-by-12 strip has perimeter 26 units. The area count stays the same whether or not the perimeter changes.
activities.insight: Area is the count of unit squares covering a region; it is distinct from perimeter and is unchanged when the same squares are rearranged.

activities.title: Label area on one rectangle, perimeter on its congruent twin
steps: On the first, mark the unit lengths all the way around the perimeter and total them.
On the second, draw the interior square units and count them for the area.
State in words how the two measurements differ, using square units for area and unit lengths for perimeter.
activities.insight: Area (surface covered, in square units) and perimeter (distance around, in unit lengths) are distinct attributes even of the very same rectangle.

activities.title: Predict then count: does longer mean bigger area?
steps: Before counting, look at two shapes — a compact block and a long spread-out strip — and predict which has the bigger area and why.
Count the covering unit squares in each shape.
Compare your prediction with the counts and explain any difference.

Answer the follow-ups: What does the area of a shape actually tell you? If you cut a shape apart and rearrange its squares into a long line, does the area change? Why? Shape B is longer than Shape A — so why doesn't 'longer' mean 'bigger area'? How is area different from the distance all the way around the edge?
activities.insight: 'Bigger area' is decided by counting covering squares, not by how far a shape stretches or how long its edge is; and area is preserved when the same squares are rearranged.

activities.title: Sort statements: about area or about perimeter?
steps: Read statements and shape comparisons and sort each into 'about area' or 'about perimeter'.
For a long-thin shape and a compact shape, decide which has the bigger area and which has the bigger perimeter, and justify each by counting.
Choose, with reasons, which of several shapes has the bigger area.
activities.insight: Learners can tell which questions concern surface covered (area) versus distance around (perimeter) and justify comparisons by counting.

checkQuestion: Show two shapes on squared paper: Shape A is a solid 3-by-4 block (12 squares) and Shape B is a long 1-by-10 strip (10 squares). Ask: 'Which shape has the bigger AREA — and how do you know?'
checkAnswer: Shape A. Area is the number of unit squares that cover a shape with no gaps or overlaps, and A is covered by 12 squares while B is covered by 10 — so A has the bigger area, 12 square units, even though B stretches further.
